newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: WOLTERS SEES DOUBLE-DIGIT GROWTH AHEAD.
newsitem.headline: WOLTERS SEES DOUBLE-DIGIT GROWTH AHEAD.

text.p: Business publisher Wolters Kluwer NV said on Friday its bottom-line earnings rose a modest six percent in 1996, but it repeated that it expected to return to its more customary double-digit earnings growth from 1997.
Net profit edged up to 479 million guilders from 452 million in 1995, despite a 47 percent increase in sales to 4.3 billion guilders, but this was right in line with market expectations.
Sales jumped mainly as a result of the early 1996 takeover of U.S. tax publisher CCH, but this also led to a write-off of 65 million guilders in goodwill.

The company had warned long ago that this accounting measure would lead to a temporary dip in earnings growth in 1996 but would not adversely affect its traditionally strong cash flow which rose 45 percent to 985 million guilders last year.

Though hardly a household name, Wolters Kluwer was recently ranked as the third most profitable company in the Financial Times Global 500 where it was also ranked as one of the top 10 media companies in terms of market capitalisation.
It operates in 25 countries, producing publications for the legal, tax, business, medical and science markets.
The company is targeting annual growth of earnings per share of at least 15 percent in the coming years.
"The target of Wolters Kluwer for growth in net earnings per fully diluted share for the years 1997-1999 is again at least 15 percent per year on average," it said.
The company raised its 1996 dividend to 2.48 guilders per share from 2.16 guilders and said it was raising its dividend payout ratio to around 35 percent from just over 30 percent.
"In view of the increasingly international spread of our shareholders, this higher structural level is more in line with current international expectations," it said.
In addition to CCH, growth was boosted by smaller acquisitions last year in legal and tax publishing, business publishing and professional training.
Excluding CCH, sales grew by 11 percent in 1996 due to a combined effect of organic growth, acquisitions and moderately favourable exchange rates.
The company's overall profit margin edged up, with income before amortisation of goodwill rising to 21.5 percent of sales from 20.7 percent in 1995.
Wolters Kluwer shares closed up 2.10 guilders at 253.60 in Amsterdam, slipping more than six guilders just after the results but then joining a broader recovery in share prices.
"We've seen recently that unless a company's figures really contain a positive surprise, the share price can react negatively," said Rabo Securities analyst Patrick Wollenberg.
Wollenberg was generally positive about the company's 1996 results and the medium-term outlook.
"CCH has been doing very well and that has allowed Wolters to make extra investments in electronic publishing," he said.
